points.html: A unit (मात्रक) of measurement (मापन) is a definite magnitude of a quantity, defined and adopted by convention or by law.

In physics, power (शक्ति) is the rate of doing work (कार्य) or of transferring heat (ऊष्मा) or electrical energy (ऊर्जा) i.e. the amount of energy transferred or converted per unit (मात्रक) time. Power (P) = Time (t)Work (W) The SI unit of power is watt, which is equal to joule per second. Power is always represented in watt (W) or kilowatt (kW).

When a force (बल) acts to move an object, then work (कार्य) done by the force is equivalent to the product of force and displacement in the direction of force . It is a scalar quantity. The SI unit (मात्रक) of work is Newton metre, which is also called as joule. Joule is also the unit of Energy (ऊर्जा).

Unit (मात्रक) of radioactivity (रेडियोधर्मिता) is defined as the activity of a quantity of radioactive material where one decay takes place per second. The SI unit of radioactivity is becquerel (Bq) and this term is named after Henri Becquerel. Curie (Ci) is the old U.S. unit (non-S.I. unit) of radioactivity. Other pairs are correctly matched.
Light (प्रकाश)-year i s a unit (मात्रक) of astronomical distance equivalent to the distance that light travels in one year, which is 9.461 × 1015 metres.
It is used as a standard for measurement (मापन) of the same kind of quantity.

The parsec (symbol: pc) is a unit (मात्रक) of length used to measure the large distances to astronomical objects outside the Solar System, approximately equal to 3.262 light (प्रकाश)-years or ~ 206265 astronomical units (au), i.e. 30.9 trillion kilometres (19.2 trillion miles). A parsec is the distance from the Sun to an astronomical object that has a parallax angle...

Any other quantity of that kind can be expressed as a multiple of the unit (मात्रक) of measurement (मापन).

Acceleration (त्वरण) is the rate of change of velocity (वेग) of an object, with respect to time. The SI unit (मात्रक) of acceleration is metre per second square (m/s 2). The SI unit of force (बल) is newton (N). The SI unit of impulse is newton second (Ns). The SI unit of work (कार्य) is joule.

Light (प्रकाश) year is not a unit (मात्रक) of measuring time, but a unit of measuring distance. The remaining pairs are correctly matched.

points.html: Mechanics : Mechanics is that area of science concerned with the behaviour of physical bodies when subjected to force (बल) or displacements and the subsequent effects of the bodies on their environment.
Weight (भार) : Weight is the force (बल) exerted on a body by gravity (गुरुत्वाकर्षण)/ force with which the Earth attracts it.

Mass (द्रव्यमान) : Mass represents the amount of matter (measure of inertia) in a particle or an object. Mass remains the same everywhere (in Classical Mechanics). It is denoted by 'm'. Difference between Weight (भार) and Mass S.N. Weight (W) Mass (m) 1. 2. 3. 4. Gravitational (गुरुत्वाकर्षण) force (बल) of Earth It is a vector (वाहक) quantity. Weight varies according to places. Its SI unit (मात्रक) is newton (N). A measurement (मापन) of the amount of matter something contains It is a scalar quantity. It is constant at every place. Its SI unit is kilogram (kg). Distance & Displacement :
In daily language Distance & Displacement are used in the same sense but in Physics both have a different meaning.
The length of a specific path travelled between two points by an object is distance.
Displacement is the shortest distance measured from the initial to the final position of an object (along a straight line) and has direction from initial to final position.

Travelled distance has only magnitude, while displacement has magnitude along with the direction. It is clear that distance is a scalar quantity and displacement is a vector (वाहक) quantity. In a course of motion, the travelled distance by an object is not zero, but the final displacement may be zero. Displacement of an object will be zero when the moving object comes to its initial point. Speed (चाल) & Velocity (वेग) :

Speed (चाल) is the distance travelled per unit (मात्रक) of time. The average speed of an object is obtained by dividing the total distance by the total time taken. ∴ Average speed = Totalt imet akenTotalt ravelledd istance It is a scalar quantity and its SI unit is metre/second.

The reading of the balance increases if the person inhales deeply. One litre of air weighs about 1.225 g. A maximal 4.8 litre breath (average vital capacity for males) weighs approximately 5.88g. Inhaled air will add to the mass (द्रव्यमान) of the man and thus his weight (भार) goes up slightly.

The scalar quantity is defined as the quantity that has only got magnitude, but not directions whereas, vector (वाहक) quantity comprises of both magnitude and directions. Displacement, velocity (वेग) and force (बल) are the examples of vector quantity while volume is a scalar quantity.

Heat (ऊष्मा) always transfer from a substance of higher temperature (तापमान) to a substance of lower temperature. Measurement (मापन) of temperature :

points.html: In general physics, a free electron (इलेक्ट्रॉन) is an electron that can move under the influence of an applied electric (and/or magnetic) field rather than remaining bound to an atom (परमाणु) or molecule (अणु).
Metals with a high availability of free electrons/mobile charge carriers (and low scattering (प्रकीर्णन)) show high electrical conductivity (चालकता).
Silver has the highest electrical conductivity (चालकता) among common metals at room temperature (तापमान); copper, gold, and aluminium are also good conductors.
Electrical conduction (चालन) is also found in some liquids (e.g., electrolytes) and in gases when the gas becomes ionized (plasma (प्लाज्मा)/discharge).

In metals, conduction (चालन) is mainly due to the motion of electrons. In electrolytic liquids, conduction is mainly due to the motion of positive and negative ions. In ionized gases, conduction occurs due to electrons and ions.

Gases are generally poor conductors under ordinary conditions, but they conduct when sufficiently ionized. Gas breakdown/discharge depends on the electric field and on conditions such as the pressure (दाब)-gap product (Paschen-type behaviour); electrical discharges/arcs can occur even at atmospheric pressure (वायुमंडलीय दाब) (e.g., lightning, arc lamps/welding). Non-conductor :
Materials with very high electrical resistivity (very few free electrons/mobile charge carriers under normal conditions) are called insulators (non-conductors).
In insulators, electrons (and ions) are usually tightly bound and do not move easily, so current is extremely small under normal conditions.

points.html: Electric Conductivity (चालकता) :
Within the atom (परमाणु), electrons nearest to the nucleus are strongly bound to the positively charged nucleus (due to protons) by electrostatic attraction.
Electrons farther from the nucleus (outer/valence electrons) are comparatively less tightly bound.
Because they are less tightly bound, such outer electrons can be removed more easily (with sufficient external energy (ऊर्जा)).
In metals, some outer electrons become delocalized in the solid and act as ‘conduction (चालन) (free) electrons’.
Free (conduction (चालन)) electrons are electrons not bound to a particular atom (परमाणु) and are free to move through the material when an external electric field is applied.

In general physics, a free electron (इलेक्ट्रॉन) is an electron that can move under the influence of an applied electric (and/or magnetic) field rather than remaining bound to an atom (परमाणु) or molecule (अणु).
Metals with a high availability of free electrons/mobile charge carriers (and low scattering (प्रकीर्णन)) show high electrical conductivity (चालकता).

Electrical conductivity (चालकता) is a measure of the amount of electric current (विद्युत धारा) which a material can carry. The most electrically conductive element (तत्व) is silver followed by copper, aluminium and iron.

Copper rods are preferred for making lightning conductor because : (i) Copper is a better conductor of electricity than iron. (ii) Copper is not easily oxidized in the presence of oxygen and water molecules while iron gets rusted. (iii) Loss of energy (ऊर्जा) is much less with a copper rod than with iron rod, as copper is a bad conductor of heat (ऊष्मा) than iron.

A person travelling in a car with closed glass windows and doors is safe from the lightening strike, because closed car behaves like a closed hollow conductor (as a Faraday cage) and electric field or charge inside a closed conductor is always zero and hence, charges cannot enter inside the car.
Materials with very high electrical resistivity (very few free electrons/mobile charge carriers under normal conditions) are called insulators (non-conductors).
In insulators, electrons (and ions) are usually tightly bound and do not move easily, so current is extremely small under normal conditions.
Under sufficiently strong electric fields, an insulator (विद्युतरोधी) may conduct due to dielectric breakdown. Semiconductor (अर्धचालक) :
A semiconductor (अर्धचालक) is a material whose electrical conductivity (चालकता) lies between that of conductors and insulators.
Its conductivity (चालकता) can increase due to temperature (तापमान) (thermal generation of charge carriers) and due to controlled impurity addition (doping).
Adding controlled impurities to a semiconductor (अर्धचालक) is called doping; doped semiconductors are called extrinsic semiconductors.
Semiconductors typically show decreasing resistance (प्रतिरोध) with increasing temperature (तापमान), opposite to most metals.
Examples: Silicon, Germanium, Selenium, Tellurium (and α-Tin as a special elemental case). Superconductivity (अतिचालकता) :
If we could achieve superconductivity (अतिचालकता) at room temperature (तापमान) then we can save billions of rupee through electric transmission without any power (शक्ति) loss.

General Science  General Studies G–142 When superconductivity (अतिचालकता) was discovered in 1911, it was found only at temperatures close to absolute zero (– 273.15°C). Ceramic oxides play a vital role in the field of research and discovery towards superconductivity (अतिचालकता). Ceramic super conductive materials contain Mercury (Hg)/Thallium (Tl), Barium (Ba), Calcium (Ca) and Copper oxide (CO). Its discovery was first reported in 1993 and its transition temperature (तापमान) (Tc) was between 94 K-135 K.

With the increase in temperature (तापमान), the conductivity (चालकता) of the semiconductor (अर्धचालक) material increases. As with increase in temperature, outermost electrons acquire energy (ऊर्जा) and hence by acquiring energy, the outermost electrons leave the shell of the atom (परमाणु). Hence, with an increase in temperature, number of carriers in the semiconductor material increases which l...

High-pressure (दाब) hydrogen-rich materials have shown very high Tc values. In 2019 it was discovered that lanthanum decahydride (LaH10) shows superconductivity (अतिचालकता) at around 250-260 K under megabar pressures of around 168-180 gigapascals (GPa).

A 2020 claim of near room-temperature (तापमान) superconductivity (अतिचालकता) in “carbonaceous sulfur hydride” was later retracted (Nature, 26 Sep 2022), and a 2023 near-ambient claim in N-doped lutetium hydride was also retracted (Nature, 7 Nov 2023). Therefore, as of March, 2026, no room temperature superconductor is confirmed at ambient conditions, and the best-confirmed very-high T c results remain in high-pressure (दाब) hydrides such as LaH10. Nuclear fission (नाभिकीय विखंडन) is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei (fission fragments) of comparable masses, usually accompanied by neutrons and gamma radiation (विकिरण).
Sometimes neutrons are absorbed by a nucleus to form a heavier isotope; this is neutron (न्यूट्रॉन) capture, not nuclear fission (नाभिकीय विखंडन).
In fission, most energy (ऊर्जा) is released as kinetic energy (heat (ऊष्मा)) of the fission fragments; the remainder is carried by neutrons and gamma rays.

points.html: Launched in 2015, the mission aims to enhance India’s technological prowess in supercomputing, foster research and development (R&D), and support scientific advancements across academia, industry, and government sectors.

NSM was set up to provide the country with supercomputing infrastructure to meet the increasing computational demands of academia, researchers, MSMEs, and startups. It is a first of its kind attempt to boost the country’s computing power (शक्ति).

The Mission envisages empowering our national academic and R&D institutions spread over the country by installing supercomputers of various capacities. Access to these supercomputers is provided through the National Knowledge Network (NKN). The NKN is another program of the government which connects academic institutions and R&D labs over a high-speed (चाल) network.
Academic and R&D institutions as well as key user departments/ministries would participate by using these facilities and develop applications of national relevance.

The Mission also includes development of highly professional High-Performance Computing (HPC) aware human resource for meeting challenges of development of these applications. HRD activities in this area are steered through five training centres at Pune, Kharagpur, Chennai, Palakkad, and Goa to expand the awareness and G–163 General Studies  General Science familiarization of supercomputing with college students and researchers.

Under NSM, as of 30 November, 2025, a total of 37 supercomputers with cumulative compute capacity of 39 Petaflops, have been deployed across various academic institutions, research organizations, and R&D labs, including prominent institutions like IISc, IITs, C-DAC, and other institutions from Tier-II and Tier III cities of the country under NSM.

The supercomputing systems commissioned under NSM have achieved an overall utilization rate of over 85%, with many systems exceeding 95%, demonstrating a high level of usage and efficiency in their computational capacity.

NSM is steered jointly by Department of Science and Technology (DST) and Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and implemented by Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC), Pune and Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru. Classification of Computer :

The MTCR seeks to limit the risks of proliferation of weapons of mass (द्रव्यमान) destruction (WMD) by controlling exports of goods and technologies that could make a contribution to delivery systems (other than manned aircraft) for such weapons. In this context, the Regime places particular focus on rockets and unmanned aerial vehicles capable of delivering a payload of at least 500 kg to a range of at least 300 km and on equipment, software, and technology for such systems.

The MTCR is not a treaty and does not impose any legally binding obligations on Partners (members). Rather, it is an informal political understanding among states that seek to limit the proliferation of missiles and missile technology. The Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Pro- liferation (HCoC) :

The Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation (HCoC) is the result of efforts of the international community to internationally regulate the area of ballistic missiles capable of carrying weapons of mass (द्रव्यमान) destruction (WMD).
The Hague Code of Conduct (HCoC), was established on 25 November, 2002 as an arrangement to prevent the proliferation of ballistic missiles.

The HCoC is the only multilateral code in the area of disarmament which has been adopted over the last years. The HCoC does not ban ballistic missiles, but calls for maximum possible restraint in the development, testing and deployment of ballistic missiles capable of delivering WMD.

Along with the MTCR, the HCoC is one of the only multilateral instruments addressing ballistic missile proliferation; the HCOC is the transparency and confidence building measure concerning the spread of ballistic missiles.

points.html: Albert Einstein (1879-1955) :

German-born physicist who developed the special and general theories of relativity and won the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1921 for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.
Einstein is generally considered the most influential physicist of the 20th Century. Einstein miracle year 1905 –
While working at the patent office, he did some of the most creative works of his life.

First Paper – He applied the quantum theory (Developed by German Physicist Max Planck) to light (प्रकाश) in order to explain the phenomenon known as the photoelectric effect, by which a material will emit electrically charged particles when hit by light.

Second Paper – Einstein's second paper of 1905, titled "On the Motion of Small Particles Suspended in a Stationary Liquid, as Required by the Molecular-Kinetic Theory of Heat (ऊष्मा)", provided a theoretical, mathematical explanation for Brownian motion. it provided crucial evidence for the existence of atoms and molecules, helping to convince skeptical physicists of their reality.

Third Paper – In the third and most famous article titled “On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies” Einstein confronted the apparent contradiction between two principal theories of physics : Isaac Newton concepts of absolute space and time and James Clerk Maxwell’s idea (via electromagnetism) that the speed (चाल) of light (प्रकाश) is a constant. To do this he introduced his Special Theory of Relativity which held that the laws of physics are the same even for objects moving in different inertial frames (i.e. at constant speeds relative to each other) and that the speed of light is constant in all inertial frames.

Fourth paper concerned the fundamental relationship between mass (द्रव्यमान) and energy (ऊर्जा). Einstein famous equation E = mc2 (where ‘c’ is the constant speed (चाल) of light (प्रकाश)) expressed this relationship.

Bose, a graduate of the University of Calcutta taught at the University of Dhaka (1921-1945) and then at Calcutta (1945-1956). Bose’s numerous scientific papers published contributed to statistical mechanics and thermoluminescence and unified field theory. Bose’s Planck’s Law and the Hypothesis of Light (प्रकाश) Quanta (1924) led Einstein to seek him out for a collaboration.
A Fellow of the Royal Society, he was awarded India’s second-highest civilian award, the Padma Vibhushan, in 1954 by the Govt. of India.

ISCA has been promoting science and inculcating the spirit of science through its multifarious activities.

The ISCA vision is to inculcate scientific temper among the common people.

The ISCA mission is to make people aware about the recent developments in science and technology and its impact on the society, to establish different centres all over India for spreading scientific knowledge through school / college programs, to provide a common platform where scientists from India and abroad can exchange their views.

Masers are used as the timekeeping device in atomic clocks, and as extremely low-noise microwave amplifiers in radio telescopes and deep space spacecraft communication ground stations.

Modern masers can be designed to generate electromagnetic waves at not only microwave frequencies but also radio and infrared frequencies. For this reason Charles Townes suggested replacing "microwave" with the word "molecular" as the first word in the acronym maser.

A liquid crystal is a thermodynamically stable phase characterized by anisotropy of properties without the existence of a three-dimensional crystal lattice, generally lying in the temperature (तापमान) range between the solid and isotropic liquid phase, hence the term mesophase.

Liquid crystal materials are unique in their properties and uses. As research into this field continues and as new applications are developed, liquid crystals will play an important role in modern technology.

Liquid crystal materials generally have several common characteristics. Among these are a rod like molecular structure, rigidity of the long axis, and strong dipole and/ or easily polarizable substituents.
Liquid crystals find wide use in liquid crystal displays, which rely on the optical properties of certain liquid crystalline substances in the presence or absence of an electric field.

Liquid crystals have a multitude of other uses. They are used for nondestructive mechanical testing of materials under stress. This technique is also used for the visualization of RF (radio frequency (आवृत्ति)) waves in waveguides. They are used in medical applications where, for example, transient pressure (दाब) transmitted by a walking foot on the ground is measured. Low molar mass (द्रव्यमान) (LMM) liquid crystals have applications including erasable optical disks, full color "electronic slides" for computer-aided drawing (CAD), and light (प्रकाश) modulators for color electronic imaging. Neutron (न्यूट्रॉन) is a neutral particle which has no electrical charge. It was discovered by Chadwick in 1932. He discovered that when Beryllium (Be) or other atoms are bombarded with high speed (चाल) particles, then electrically neutral particles emerges from these atoms and such neutral particles are known as neutrons.

The particles that are smaller than the atoms are called sub- atomic particles. The three main sub-atomic particles that form an atom (परमाणु) are protons, neutrons and electrons. Deuteron contains a proton (प्रोटॉन) and a neutron (न्यूट्रॉन).
Atoms of different elements are with different atomic number.

The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom (परमाणु)’s nucleus is known as its mass (द्रव्यमान) number.
It is used as the nucleon count and approximates the atomic mass (द्रव्यमान) of a nuclide in atomic mass units.
Mass (द्रव्यमान) number of an atom (परमाणु) = No. of protons + No. of neutrons in nucleus of an atom.
It represents the total number of nucleons in the nucleus of an atom (परमाणु).
The mass (द्रव्यमान) number is not a fundamental character of the element (तत्व).

In particle physics, an elementary particle or fundamental particle is a subatomic particle with no sub-structure, thus not composed of other particles. Particles currently thought to be elementary include the fundamental fermions (quarks, leptons, antiquarks and antileptons) as well as fundamental bosons.

Neutrinos are one of the most abundant particles in the universe. Because they have very little interaction with matter, however, they are incredibly difficult to detect.

Different element (तत्व)’s atom (परमाणु) with the same number of neutrons are called Isoneutronic or Isotones. Radioactivity (रेडियोधर्मिता) is a nuclear phenomenon in which there is a spontaneous emission of radiations from the nuclei of atoms during their decay. In other words, radioactive decay is the process by which an unstable atomic nucleus loses energy (ऊर्जा) by radiation (विकिरण). Unstable nuclei that exist in nature are said to undergo natural radioactivity, and the man made unstable nuclei undergo artificial radioactivity.
The elements with such atoms have spontaneous disintegration character.
Such elements are called radioactive substances.
α particles, β particles and γ rays are emitted by radioactive nuclei. These three types of radiation (विकिरण) are called ionizing radiation.
Radioactivity (रेडियोधर्मिता) is a nuclear phenomenon, not a chemical reaction.
It was discovered by Henri Becquerel in Uranium.
In 1898 Marie Curie and her husband Pierre Curie discovered a radioactive element (तत्व) Polonium.

The Isotopes (समस्थानिक) are a set of nuclides/atoms having the same number of protons, but a different number of neutrons. In other words, the same atomic number (Z) but having different mass (द्रव्यमान) number (A). Each individual isotope has a separate nuclei. The Isotopes that are unstable and undergo radioactive decay are called radioisotopes.

points.html: Matter is defined as anything that occupies space and exhibits rest mass (द्रव्यमान) or inertia.

In physical changes no new substances are formed; the substance retains the same chemical composition while only its physical properties change. Physical changes may be reversible; some physical changes are irreversible, even though no new substance is formed.

In our daily life, we encounter many changes in our surroundings, though we do not notice them, such as souring of milk, rusting of iron, stretching of a rubber band, bread becoming toast, melting of wax, etc.
All these changes that take place around us are either a physical change or chemical change. Physical Changes
Physical changes, are the changes that change the physical traits of the substance, without making any change in their internal structure.

points.html: Several major attempts were made for classification of elements. Some of them are as follows - (i) Prout Hypothesis (1815-16) –
William Prout observed that the atomic weights that had been measured for the elements known at that time appeared to be whole multiples of the atomic weight (भार) of hydrogen.

He hypothesized that the hydrogen atom (परमाणु) was the only truly fundamental object, which he called protyle and that the atoms of other elements were actually groupings of various numbers of hydrogen atoms.

Later, more precise measurements of atomic weights showed many values were not exact integer multiples of hydrogen, so chemists rejected this simple form of the hypothesis, even though a modified ‘whole-number rule’ for isotopes (समस्थानिक) remains approximately valid. (ii) Dobereiner’s Law of Triads (1829) –

According to this law, when chemically analogous elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic weight (भार), they formed well-marked group of three called ‘Triads’, in which the atomic weight of middle element (तत्व) was nearly equal to the arithmetic mean of the other.

Periodic Table or Periodic table of elements is a tabular arrangement of the chemical elements, arranged by atomic number, electron (इलेक्ट्रॉन) configuration and recurring chemical properties, whose structure shows periodic trends. Need for classification of Elements :
Before the beginning of the 18 th century, only a few elements were known, so it was quite easy to study and remember the properties of those elements and their compounds individually.

Later on, with the growing number of known elements, it became more and more difficult to study their properties individually, therefore the need for their systematic classification was felt. Development of Periodic Table :
Several major attempts were made for classification of elements. Some of them are as follows - (i) Prout Hypothesis (1815-16) –
William Prout observed that the atomic weights that had been measured for the elements known at that time appeared to be whole multiples of the atomic weight (भार) of hydrogen.

He hypothesized that the hydrogen atom (परमाणु) was the only truly fundamental object, which he called protyle and that the atoms of other elements were actually groupings of various numbers of hydrogen atoms.

Later, more precise measurements of atomic weights showed many values were not exact integer multiples of hydrogen, so chemists rejected this simple form of the hypothesis, even though a modified ‘whole-number rule’ for isotopes (समस्थानिक) remains approximately valid. (ii) Dobereiner’s Law of Triads (1829) –

The most abundant element (तत्व) in the Universe is Hydrogen, which makes up about 3/4 of all matter. Helium makes up most of the remaining 1/4. Thus, it is clear that hydrogen is the most common and abundant element in the Universe. While the most abundant element in the Earth's crust is Oxygen making up 46.6% of Earth's crust.

All elements present in a group generally have similar electronic configuration in their valence shell and have the same number of valence electrons for main-group elements; transition metals are an important exception. Periods :
There are seven horizontal rows in the modern periodic table.
The elements in a period have consecutive atomic numbers.
The periods have been numbered from 1 to 7 (Arabic numerals).

In each period a new shell starts filling up. The period number is also the number of shells that starts filling up as we move from left to right across the period. (a) The first period is the shortest period of all. It contains only two elements – H and He. (b) The second and third periods are called short-periods each with 8 elements. (c) The 4th & 5th periods are called long periods each with 18 elements. (d) The 6th & 7th periods are very long periods; both presently have 32 known elements. Types of Elements :

points.html: The acid (अम्ल) name comes from Latin acidus which means sour and refers to the sharp odour and sour taste of many acids.
According to Arrhenius, acid (अम्ल) is a compound (यौगिक) that can increase the hydrogen-ion (H +/Hydronium-ion H 3O+) concentration in aqueous solution.

According to Bronsted - Lowry concept, acid (अम्ल) is defined as any hydrogen containing material which can donate a proton (प्रोटॉन) (hydron) to other substances. Properties of Acids : (i) Acids in solution have a pH below 7.0 (at about 25°C). (ii) Taste is sour. (iii) Releases hydrogen-ion (H+) in water. (iv) An acid turns blue litmus paper into red. (v) Chemicals or substances having the property of an acid are said to be acidic. Classification of acids :

Acids are divided into two main classes : I. Strong acids : These are completely ionized in water. They are very corrosive and can cause severe skin burns. Examples are hydrochloric acid (अम्ल) (HCl), Sulfuric acid (H2SO4) and nitric acid (HNO3). II. Weak acids : These are partially ionized in water. They are mildly corrosive and normally do not affect the skin. Examples are citric acid, acetic acid, tartaric acid etc. Sources of Some Natural Acids S.N. Name of Acid Source 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. Tartaric Acid Acetic acid (Ethanoic acid) Citric acid Oxalic acid Lactic acid Malic acid Ascorbic acid (Vitamin (विटामिन) C) Formic acid Grapes, Tamarind, Some citrus fruits, Bananas Vinegar Lemon, Orange and commonly in all citrus fruits Tomato, Spinach Curd Apple Amla, Guava, Papaya, Orange Stings of ants and Stinging Nettle (a plant) Uses of Acids : (i) Tartaric acid, lactic acid, acetic acid and malic acid are edible acids. (ii) Oxalic acid is used to remove the rust/iron stains on clothes. (iii) Conc.-Nitric acid is used in the preparation of explosive substances and for seperation of silver from gold-silver alloys. (iv) Aqua regia is a mixture (मिश्रण) of three-part of conc-hydrochloric acid and one part of conc-nitric acid (3 conc-HCl : 1 conc- HNO3). It has capacity to dissolve platinum and gold. It is also known as Royal water. It is primarily used to produce chloroauric acid for refining the highest quality of gold. It is also used in laboratories to remove trace amounts of organic compounds and trace metals from glassware. (v) Carbonic acid is (through carbonation of water from added CO2) present in soda and many soft drinks. (vi) Phosphoric acid is used as acidulant in Coca-Cola. (vii) Certain acids are used as drugs. Acetylsalicylic acid (Aspirin) is used as a pain-killer and for bringing down fever. Role of Acids in Human Body :

Acids play important roles in the human body. (i) The hydrochloric acid (अम्ल) present in the stomach (आमाशय) helps in the digestion (पाचन). (ii) Amino acids are the structural unit (मात्रक) of protein. For the synthesis of protein, amino acids are required. Protein is very essential for the growth and repair of body cells. (iii) Fatty acids are also required for growth and repair of body tissue. (iv) Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are essential for all known forms of life. Genes/DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) are responsible for transmitting of traits to offsprings from parents; RNA (ribonucleic acid) is involved in protein synthesis. (v) The carbonic acid/bicarbonate (H 2CO3/ HCO3
) buffer system is essential for the maintenance of pH equilibrium in the body. Base (क्षार) :
According to Arrhenius , a base (क्षार) is a compound (यौगिक) that increases the concentration of hydroxide ions (OH –) in aqueous solution.

According to Bronsted-Lowry concept, base (क्षार) is any substance that can accept a proton (प्रोटॉन) (hydron) from an acid (अम्ल)/ proton donor. Properties of Bases : (i) Bases have a bitter taste. (ii) Bases feel slippery. (iii) Bases conduct electricity in aqueous solution, because they consist of charged particles in solution. G–382 General Studies  General Science (iv) A water-soluble base is called an alkali if it produces OH– ions in water. (v) Bases in solution have a pH above 7.0 (at about 25°C). (vi) An alkali turns red litmus into blue. Some bases and their uses are as follows : (a) Calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)2–Slaked Lime (Limewater is saturated aqueous solution of this) (b) Ammonium hydroxide NH 4OH (Aqueous ammonia)–to clean glass windows. (c) Sodium hydroxide NaOH–used to prepare soap. (d) Potassium hydroxide KOH – used to prepare soap. (e) Magnesium hydroxide Mg(OH)2 – Its aqueous suspension is known as milk of magnesia, a common antacid. It is used to remove the acidity of the stomach (आमाशय) and also as a laxative. pH Scale :

points.html: In organic chemistry, a hydrocarbon (हाइड्रोकार्बन) is an organic compound (यौगिक) consisting entirely of hydrogen and carbon.
Hydrocarbons from which one hydrogen atom (परमाणु) has been removed are univalent substituent groups called hydrocarbyls, e.g. Methyl, phenyl etc.
In hydrocarbons the carbon atoms join together to form the framework of the compound (यौगिक) and the hydrogen atoms attach to them in many different configurations.
Hydrocarbons are the principal constituents of petroleum and natural gas.
Hydrocarbons serve as fuels and lubricants as well as raw materials for the production of plastics, fibres, rubbers, solvents, explosives and industrial chemicals.

Many hydrocarbons occur in nature. In addition to making up fossil fuels, they are present in trees and plants. For example in the form of pigments called carotene (C40Hx e.g. β-carotene C40H56) that occur in carrots and green leaves.

points.html: The hydrocarbons, which contain carbon atoms linked on the non-cyclic (acyclic) open-chain are known as open- chain hydrocarbons. In these hydrocarbons, the chain of carbon atoms is not cyclic.
Open-chain hydrocarbons are further divided into (i) Saturated hydrocarbons (ii) Unsaturated hydrocarbons (i) Saturated hydrocarbons (Alkanes):
Those hydrocarbons, in which the carbon atoms are bonded to each other with a single covalent bond (–C–C–) are called a cyclic saturated hydrocarbons. They are also known as alkanes.
They follow the general formula CnH2n+2 (–ane suffix). For example-methane, ethane, propane, etc.
They are also known as paraffin because these are less reactive in normal conditions with acids and other reagents (Parum = too little, Affinis = related → little affinity). Methane (CH4) :
Methane is the first member of open chain saturated hydrocarbons.

Methane is the primary constituent of natural gas and it is released into the atmosphere from crude oil production and some industrial activities. More of it is released from biological processes. It is also known as Marsh gas due to its production in the wetland by decomposition of organic materials by anaerobic archaea (methanogens). points.html: Alcohol is an organic compound (यौगिक) with a hydroxyl (–OH) functional group attached to a saturated carbon atom (परमाणु). Because –OH is the functional group of all alcohols, we often represent alcohols by the general formula R-OH where R is an alkyl group.
In other words, the hydroxyl derivatives of alkenes/ aliphatic hydrocarbons are termed as alcohols.

Condensed/structural formula and name of some alcohols are as follows : (i) Methyl Alcohol (Methanol) – CH3OH (ii) Ethyl Alcohol (Ethanol) – C2H5OH (iii) n-Propyl Alcohol – CH3CH2CH2OH (iv) Isopropyl Alcohol – (CH3)2CHOH (v) n-Butyl Alcohol – CH3 (CH2)2CH2OH (vi) Isobutyl Alcohol – (CH3)2CHCH2OH Methyl Alcohol (Methanol or Carbinol) :
Its chemical formula is CH3OH.
It acquired the name wood alcohol or wood naphtha because it was once produced primarily by the destructive distillation of wood.
Today it is mainly produced by hydrogenation of carbon monoxide.
It is the simplest alcohol, consisting of a methyl group linked to a hydroxyl group.
It is light (प्रकाश), volatile, colourless, flammable liquid with a distinctive odour similar to that of ethanol (Ethyl alcohol).
Methyl alcohol (CH 3OH) is also called wood spirit. It is obtained by the destructive distillation of wood.

It is used in the preparation of the methylated spirit. A mixture (मिश्रण) of methyl alcohol and ethyl alcohol is known as methylated spirit or denatured alcohol, which is not suitable for drinking.

The mixture (मिश्रण) of methyl alcohol (40%) and water (60%) is used earlier in radiators of automobiles as antifreeze . Modern automobile engine coolants are predominantly ethylene-glycol based. Ethyl Alcohol (Ethanol) :

Barley, water, hops and yeast are the four magic ingredients that are required for making beer. Other grains like maize, rice, rye and wheat are also used in making beer. Whisky is also made from fermented barley grains.

The word ‘Science’ comes from the Latin word ‘scientia’, meaning ‘knowledge’.
Science is the systematic knowledge of the physical or material world gained through observation and experimentation.
Science has been classified into– (1) Natural Sciences and (2) Social Sciences.
The natural sciences comprise the physical sciences, Earth and space sciences, and life (biological) sciences; life sciences (biology) are further divided into many branches and sub-branches.

Lamarck and Treviranus introduced the term ‘biology’ independently in modern sense in 1802. Branches and Subbranches of Biology Zoology – Detailed study of the members of the animal kingdom and animal life in general. Botany – Detailed study of plants and their life. Palaeontology – The study of history of life on Earth as based on fossils. Fossils are preserved remains, impressions, or traces of plants, animals, and other organisms from the geologic past; they may be preserved in Earth’s crust and also by processes such as drying, freezing, and entrapment in amber or asphalt. Palaeobotany – Study of plant fossils. Ecology – The branch of biology that deals with the relation of organisms to one another and to their physical surroundings. Genetics – The study of heredity (आनुवंशिकता) or how the characteristics of living things are transmitted from one generation to the next. In living organisms, DNA is the genetic material. Pedology – It is the study of soils in their natural environment. It deals with pedogenesis, soil morphology and soil classification. Biometry – It is also known as biostatistics. It is the development and application of statistical and mathematical methods to analyse the data results from biological observations and phenomenon. Phrenology – The detailed study of the shape and size of the cranium as a supposed indication of character and mental abilities. Anthology – Study of flowers. Main Terminologies and related by-products Apiculture – The raising and care of bees for honey and other hive products and agricultural purposes (pollination services, including cross pollination). Aviculture – The breeding and rearing of birds. Aquaculture – The farming of aquatic organisms–fish, molluscs, crustaceans and aquatic plants–for food and other commercial/public purposes, often with intervention to enhance production. Algaculture – A form of aquaculture involving the farming of algae. Algae can be used in wastewater treatment and nutrient recovery; harvested algal biomass can be used as fertilizer (उर्वरक). Phytoplankton are free-floating microscopic algae (often referred to as microalgae) and, in many classifications, include cyanobacteria in sunlit waters. Pisciculture – The controlled breeding and rearing of fishes. Agriculture – The science or practice of farming, including cultivation of the soil for the growing of crops and the rearing of animals to provide food, wool and other products. Sericul ture – The production of silk and the rearing of silkworms for this purpose. Silviculture – Silviculture is the practice of controlling the growth, composition, health and quality of forests to meet diverse needs and values. Spongiculture – The cultivation and growing of (marine) sponges. Horticulture – Horticulture is the science and art of growing fruits, vegetables, flowers and crops like spices/condiments and other plantation crops. Floriculture – Floriculture or flower farming, is a discipline of horticulture concerned with the cultivation of flowering and ornamental plants for gardens and for floristry, comprising the floral industry. Olericulture – Olericulture is the science of vegetables growing, dealing with the culture of non-woody (herbaceous) plants for food. Arboriculture – Cultivation and management of trees and shrubs. Pomology – The science that deals with fruit and fruit growing. Agronomy – A branch of agriculture dealing with crop production and soil management. Vermiculture – The cultivation of earthworms, especially in order to use them to convert organic waste into fertilizer (vermicompost). Oyster culture – The breeding and farming of oysters (primarily for food). Pearls are produced through pearl culture using pearl oysters. Heliculture – It is also known as snail farming. It is the process of raising land snails especially for human use, either to use their flesh to eat or to obtain snail slime for use in cosmetics and snail eggs for human consumption as a type of caviar. Viticulture – Cultivation and harvesting of grapes. Mariculture – Mariculture is a specialized branch of aqua- culture involving the cultivation of marine organisms (animal and plant) for food and other products. Moriculture – Moriculture is the science of mulberry cultivation for silk production, because silkworm (Bombyx mori) is reared on mulberry leaves. Citriculture – Cultivation of citrus fruit trees. Vegeculture – Agricultural systems producing mainly vegetatively propagated root and tuber crops; crops are reproduced asexually by planting parts of the parent plant. Aeroponics – A plant-cultivation technique without soil, in which the roots hang suspended in the air while nutrient solution is delivered to them in the form of a fine mist. Aeroculture – A method of growing plants without soil by suspending them above sprays that constantly moisten the roots with water and nutrients. Hydroponics – It is the cultivation of plants in nutrient enriched water, with or without the mechanical support of an inert medium (e.g. soil).

Several hypotheses have been proposed regarding the origin of life on Earth. The ‘Oparin–Haldane Hypothesis’ is a foundational early framework for chemical evolution (जैव विकास), but the detailed pathway of abiogenesis is not settled into a single universally accepted model. Oparin-Haldane Hypothesis of Origin of Life :

According to this hypothesis, life originated on early Earth through physico chemical processes: atoms combined to form molecules; these reacted to produce simple inorganic and organic compounds; organic compounds then gave rise to macromolecules and increasingly organized systems that eventually led to the first living system or cells.

points.html: Thus, according to this hypothesis ‘life’ originated upon our Earth spontaneously from non-living matter. First inorganic compounds and then organic compounds were formed in accordance with ever-changing environmental conditions. The hypothesis places ‘origin of life’ within chemical evolution (जैव विकास) operating under early-Earth conditions that differed from present conditions.

Hypothesis given by Oparin about origin of life is also known as Oparin’s chemical-evolution (जैव विकास) / ‘primordial soup’ formulation; influenced by dialectical materialism which was published in his book 'Origin of Life'.

Modern discussions treat origin-of-life studies as involving prebiotic chemical evolution (जैव विकास) and subsequent biological evolution, with multiple competing hypotheses for key steps. A. Chemical Evolution (Chemogeny) :

Among the given options, blue-green algae (शैवाल) is the oldest organism on Earth. They obtain their energy (ऊर्जा) through photosynthesis (प्रकाश संश्लेषण). They are also known as cyanobacteria. By producing gaseous oxygen as a by-product of photosy- nthesis, they played a greater role in dramatically changing life forms on Earth by stimulating biodiversity.

Hugo De Vries is known for his mutation (उत्परिवर्तन) theory of evolution (जैव विकास). According to him, new species are not formed by continuous variations but by the sudden appearance of variations, which he named as mutations. He stated that mutations are heritable and persist in successive generations.

The Mesozoic Era is the age of the dinosaurs and lasted almost 180 million years from approximately 250 to 65 million years ago. This era includes three well known periods, called the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.

points.html: The Mesozoic Era is the age of the dinosaurs and lasted almost 180 million years from approximately 250 to 65 million years ago. This era includes three well known periods, called the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.

Plant taxonomy (वर्गिकी) is the science of classifying, naming, and identifying plants, organizing them into groups based on shared characteristics and evolutionary relationships. Plant taxonomy uses a hierarchical system to classify plants, with each level representing a group of organisms with shared characteristics :  Kingdom : The broadest level, encomp...

Bacteria (जीवाणु) are microscopic living organisms. Most of the bacterias are just 0.5 to 5.0 micron (µ) in size but some of them are about 0.5 mm or more in size. Some of the microscopic organisms can be seen by a compound (यौगिक) microscope as it can magnify an object up to 1500-2000 times.

Bacteria (जीवाणु) have a wide range of diets. Some are heterotrophs and others are autotrophs. Most heterotrophic bacteria are saprobes (they absorb dead organic material like rotting flesh). Some of these parasitic bacteria kill their host while others help their host. Autotrophic bacteria make their own food, either by photosynthesis (प्रकाश संश्लेषण) (which uses sunlight,...

Bacteria (जीवाणु) are single-celled microbes. They are unicellular organisms consists of prokaryotic cell (कोशिका). Their cell structure is simple than that of other organisms as there is no nucleus or membrane bound organelles. Bacteria are universal, can be found everywhere. There are some harmful bacteria that can cause illness and disease. There are other bacter...

Starfish or Sea stars are star-shaped echinoderms belonging to the class Asteroidea. Jellyfish (Cnidaria) and Hagfish (Cyclostomata) are also not true fishes. Seahorse is the name given to 45 species of small marine fish in the genus Hippocampus which is a bony fish.

The sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) is the largest of the toothed whales with males growing up to 20 metres in length. The mass (द्रव्यमान) of sperm whales ranges between 35 to 45 tons. Females only weigh about 1/3 of the males.

Echidnas, sometimes known as spiny anteaters, belong to the family Tachyglossidae in the monotreme order of egg-laying mammals. The four extant species, together with the Platypus are the only surviving members of that order and are the only living mammals that lay eggs. Their diet consists of ants and termites but they are not closely related with...

Bats are the mammals of the order Chiroptera whose forelimbs form webbed wings, making them the only mammals naturally capable of true and sustained flight. Bat does not belong to the group aves (birds).
Dingoes are commonly found throughout Australia and in scattered groups across south-east Asia. Its scientific name is Canis lupus dingo. Dingoes do not bark but howl like wolves.
The bear which we see commonly performing on streets is sloth bear.
The Chimpanzee, Parrot and Dolphin can be trained to use language with some success but a dog can not be trained to use language.

The gorilla, chimpanzee, and orangutan are called great apes in recognition of their comparatively large size and humanlike features. The gibbons are called lesser apes. They are smallest, cleanest and gentlest man like an ape.

Metamorphosis is a biological process by which an animal physically develops after birth or hatching, involving a conspicuous and relatively abrupt change in the animal’s body structure through cell (कोशिका) growth and differentiation. Thyroid hormone (हार्मोन) controls remodelling of the tadpole intestine (आंत) during the climax of amphibian metamorphosis. During the meta...

Amphibians and most reptiles have a heart (हृदय) with three chambers– two atria and a single ventricle. The heart of the frog has three chambers, one ventricle and two atria. Fish has two chambered heart while monkey and crocodile has four chambered heart.

Amphibians (such as frogs) have a three-chambered heart (हृदय) (two atria and one ventricle). In a single ventricle, oxygen- ated and deoxygenated blood partially mix, which their body can tolerate. ‘Two-chambered heart’ (one atrium + one ventricle) is a characteristic of fishes, not amphibians. Therefore, Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

All members of the deer family except for the musk deer, all of the equine family (including zebras), camels, giraffes, elephants, rhinoceroses, whales, some birds (such as doves), rats and some fish do not have gallbladder.
Among the given options except Jackal, all are hooves animals. Jackal is the species of canidae. The scientific name of common Jackal is Canis aureus. The feet of Jackals are padded with nails.
Nilgai is the largest Asian antelope (deer-like) species. Antelope are creatures having strong permanent horns. There are more than 90 species of antelope.
An octopus is a cephalopod mollusc of the order octopoda, also known as devilfish. It has two eyes and four pairs of arms and like other cephalopods, it is bilaterally symmetric.
Invertebrates are the animals that do not have a backbone. The colossal squid is the largest invertebrate. It's maximum size is 12-14 metre.

Spiders belong to a group of animals called 'Arachnids'. Arachnids are creatures with two body segments, eight legs and no wings or antennae. All spiders are predators and many eat each other. Rest three options are insects. They have six legs, while spider has eight legs. Thus spider is not an insect.

Spider silk is protein fiber spun by spiders. It is also known as 'Gossamer silk'. Spider silk is an extremely strong material. It is one of the most miraculous natural substances on Earth. Most building materials are either strong or elastic, but spider silk is both. It has been often described as stronger than steel (which is not quite accurate, ...

Lac is the scarlet resinous secretion of a number of species of lac insects, of which the most commonly cultivated species is Kerria lacca. Cultivation begins when a farmer gets a stick (brood lac) that contains eggs ready to hatch and ties it to the tree to be infested.Thousands of lac insects colonize the branches of the host trees and secrete th...

Among the given options silk, lac and honey are obtained from insects, while pearl is produced within the soft tissue of a living shelled mollusk or another animal such as fossil conulariids. The most valuable pearls occur spontaneously in the wild (natural pearls which are rare), while cultured or farmed pearls are obtained from bivalve mollusks, ...

Cockroaches have white or colourless blood because they lack haemoglobin in their blood. Cockroaches do not use hemoglobin (हीमोग्लोबिन) to carry oxygen. In fact their bloodstream is not used to carry oxygen either. They use a system of tubes called tracheae to bring the oxygen and remove carbon dioxide from their tissues.

Earthworms improve soil fertility and soil health; therefore, they are called ‘friends of farmers’. Earthworms positively affect soil structure, increase organic matter, and improve water infiltration. Hence, statement 1 is correct. In earthworms, generally five pairs of heart (हृदय)-like pulsating blood vessels (aortic arches which acts as hearts) are fo...

Statement 1 is correct. Dolphins and whales are aquatic mammals. They do not breathe through gills under water; they breathe air. They use the blowhole (nostril) located on the top of the head and come to the surface to exhale and inhale. Statement 2 is also correct. Earthworms do not have any specialized respiratory organs (lungs (फेफड़े)/gills). They carr...

The largest brain (मस्तिष्क) belongs to the sperm whale : about 7 kg (17.5 pounds). The blue whale, the largest animal on the planet, being twice longer and thrice heavier, has a brain weighing about 5 kg (12.5 pounds). Human brain has an average weight (भार) of about 2.7 pounds (1.2 kg), variations between 1.1 and 1.4 kg being considered normal. Our brain represen...

Only female mosquitoes suck the blood of warm-blooded vertebrate birds and mammals and live on them as an ectoparasite. The male mosquitoes do not suck blood, they survive by feeding on flowers and fruit juices. Occasionally, females may also suck juices. Generally, female mosquitoes are larger than male mosquitoes. That is why option (d) is the co...

Among the given animals, Kangaroo rat can live for the longest duration without drinking water. The Kangaroo rat is a rodent native to the desert areas of North America. The Kangaroo rat adapted to live in the desert climate because it produces the most concentrated urine in all mammals. Their kidneys concentrate the urine so much that it becomes a...

Poisonous (Venomous) fangs of a snake are modified form of maxillary teeth. There are 1-3 pairs (usually 1 pair) of long, curved, sharp and pointed maxillary teeth attached to the poison glands of the upper jaw of a snake.

Rafflesia plant with no leaves, no roots, no stem is the biggest flower in the world .It sounds like the stuff of comic books or science fiction. ‘It is perhaps the largest and most magnificent flower in the world’ was how Sir Stamford Raffles described his discovery in 1818 of Rafflesia Arnoldii, modestly named after himself and his companion, sur...

Pitcher plants or Nepenthes are able to synthesize their food by the process of photosynthesis (प्रकाश संश्लेषण), hence they are autotrophs. Usually, they grow on soils deficient in nitrogenous compounds and fulfill their required nitrogen by digesting insects. Other options are correctly matched.

Nepenthes are insectivorous pitcher plant. Nepenthes species are perennial herbaceous plants and frequently grow in very acidic soil, though some are epiphytes. All the species are carnivorous plants that capture insects and other prey by means of modified pitcher-shaped leaves that function as passive pitfall traps.
Nependthes khasiana is India's only pitcher plant and is named after the Khasi Hill region of Meghalaya. They are mostly found in Garo, Khasi and Jaintia hills region of Meghalaya.

Turmeric is obtained from the modified stem (rhizome) of the plant. It is a member of the curcuma botanical group, which is part of a ginger family of herbs, the Zingiberaceae. Its botanical name is Curcuma longa. All curcumas are perennial plants native to southern Asia. They grow in warm humid climates and thrive only in temperatures above 60o F ...
The sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is a dicotyledonous plant that belongs to the family Convolvulaceae. Sweet potato is a modified root cultivated by vegetative propagation.
Sugarcane, potato, and ginger are modified stems i.e., their storage organ is stem, while the storage organ of sweet potato is root. It is developed by radicle.
Among the given options turnip, carrot and sweet potato are modified roots while ginger is a modified stem.

Cloves are the aromatic closed, dried floral buds, which is used in Ayurvedic medicines, making food and as an anodyne for dental emergencies. The botanical name of clove tree is Syzygium aromaticum (Eugenia caryophyllata) which belongs to Myrtaceae family. Cloves are native of Indonesia and used as a spice in cuisines all over the world. The clove...

Saffron is a spice derived from the flower of Crocus sativus, commonly known as the 'Saffron Crocus'. Saffron is obtained from the styles and stigmas of the flower of Crocus sativus. Other options are correctly matched.
Saffron is obtained from the gynoecium parts (stigma and styles) of the flower of Crocus sativus which are seed forming parts of flower.
The edible part of the potato is tuber (modified stem), not root. Thus, option (c) is not correctly matched. Other options are correctly matched.

Lychee is a juicy fruit belonging to the soapberry family. The fruit grows on an evergreen tree, with pinnate leaves. It is a drupe (like a plum, a cherry, or a mango), externally covered by a pink-red rough textured rind, easily removable.

Garlic is made up of sulphuric compounds (Allyl methyl sulphide) that render the pungent smell to it. It is also used as diaphoretic, diuretic, expectorant and for treating blood pressure (रक्तचाप) (दाब) and heart (हृदय) disease.
Sulfenic acid (अम्ल) found in onions irritates lachrymal glands and produces tears in eyes.

Chillies are valued principally for their high pungency and colour. Pungency in chillies is due to the active constituent 'capsaicin', an alkaloid which is extracted from chillies and is also used in the medicine. The molecular formula of capsaicin is C18H27NO3.
Red chillies are hot because they contain capsaicin. Its chemical formula is C18H27NO3.
Fructose is also known as fruit sugar. This type of sugar is mainly found in fruits. Fructose is a monosaccharide.

The mulberry fruit is also known as the sorosis. Sorosis is a multiple fleshy fruit that is derived from the ovaries of multiple flowers. The seeds are achenes, on the outside of a fleshy fruit. Pineapple and Ficus are also the examples of Sorosis fruit.

The fibres of sunn, hemp, and jute are obtained from stems, while cotton is obtained from the fruit of the cotton plant, called cotton balls. Cotton fibres are classified into two types namely lint and fuzz respectively. Lint fibre is more important for the commercial purpose than fuzz fibre.

Triticale is the first man-made cereal crop. It has been obtained by crossing wheat (Triticum) with rye (Secale) in laboratories during the late 19th century in Scotland and Germany. Though the Triticale is a cross between wheat and rye, it is self-pollinating (similar to wheat) and not cross-pollinating (like rye).

Term Temperature (तापमान) Adaptation Status Eurythermal Plants/organisms that can survive across a very wide temperature range Stenothermal Organisms that survive only in a narrow temperature range Microthermal Organisms tolerant of low temperatures Hekistothermal Cold-tolerant organisms found in polar regions Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

Desert plants have the capability to complete their life-cycle even in a dry atmosphere. The root system of these plants become longer in search of water from the soil and their stems are small, adapted and underground sometimes. Plant varieties that have adapted by developing very long roots are collectively known as phreatophytes.
A succulent is a plant that stores water for times when water is not available to it. Succulent plants are generally found in arid environments such as deserts and semi-deserts.

Hydrophytes or aquatic plants are plants that have adapted to live in an aquatic environment. Plants growing on saline soils or water are called halophytes (salt (लवण)-loving plants). They grow in saline semi-deserts, mangroove swamps, marshes and sloughs and seashores.
Nepenthes are not hydrophytes. They are tropical pitcher plants and a genus of carnivorous plant. Other pairs are correctly matched.

Weeping jelly is most often caused by an excess of acid (अम्ल) in the fruit or recipe in general. So statement 1 is correct. Acetobacter diazotrophicus is more suitable for sugarcane crop than other biofertilizers. Therefore statement 2 is incorrect. A halophyte is a plant that grows in waters of high salinity, therefore, statement 3 is also wrong. Dorman...

Plants and animals that live on land are called terrestrial organisms, and their habitats are known as terrestrial habitats. These are the natural environments where terrestrial organisms live, providing them with the necessary resources for survival, such as food, water, shelter, and space. These include diverse environments like forests, grasslan...
Producers or autotrophs are the intermediaries between Biotic and abiotic components of the environment.

Autotrophs are the producers in a food chain such as plants on land or algae (शैवाल) in water, in contrast to heterotrophs as consumers of autotrophs. Saprotroph, a term used for organisms which obtain nutrients from dead organic matter (this term commonly applies to fungi). A herbivore is an animal anatomically and physiologically adapted to eating plant ...

Lakes and rivers are frozen when the outer temperature (तापमान) decreases below the freezing point in winters. But only the upper layer freezes in this condition. Water remains in liquid form below the upper layer. So fishes and other aquatic creatures can survive even in a frozen lake.
Red apples get their colour from anthocyanin pigment.

The red colour of tomato (Lycopersicon esculentum) fruit is due to the carotenoid pigment lycopene. The red colour formation in the apple skin is due to the formation of anthocyanin pigments. The red-orange colour of carrot is due to the pigment β-Carotene.

The botanical name of papaya is ‘Carica papaya’. It is rich in carotene, which is a precursor of vitamin (विटामिन) A. The papain enzyme (एंजाइम) presented in papaya is helpful in digestion (पाचन) of protein. The yellow colour of papaya is due to presence of caricaxanthin.
Yeasts, moulds (molds) and mushrooms are examples of fungi. Fungi is the plural word for fungus (कवक). Fungi lack chlorophyll and vascular bundle.

points.html: The cell (कोशिका) (from Latin Cella– meaning 'small room') is the basic structural, functional and biological unit (मात्रक) of all known living organisms.
A cell (कोशिका) is the smallest unit (मात्रक) of life. Cells are often called the ‘building blocks’ of life.
The study of cells is called cell (कोशिका) biology or cellular biology.

The cell (कोशिका) consists of cytoplasm enclosed within a plasma (प्लाज्मा) membrane. Cytoplasm contains many biomolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids, while the plasma membrane is mainly lipids and proteins.
The number of cells in plants and animals varies from species to species. Adult human of 70 kg contain around 30 trillion (3 × 1013) cells.
Most plant and animal cells are visible only under a microscope, with dimensions between 1 to 100 micrometres.
Cells were discovered by Robert Hooke in 1665 (detailed description in a book written by him– Micrographia).

Cell (कोशिका) theory, first developed in 1839, by Schleiden and Schwann. According to their theory, all living organisms are composed of one or more cells and the cell is the most basic unit (मात्रक) of life. Virchow (1855) added that all new cells arise only from pre-existing cells.

Mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association formed between certain fungi and the roots of higher plants. It helps the plant-especially by increasing the absorption of phosphorus, nitrogen, and other micronutrients. Plants with mycorrhiza also get protection from root-borne diseases and from some harmful soil microorganisms.

Lichens are sensitive to atmospheric pollution (especially sulphur dioxide, etc.); therefore, they are widely used as reliable bioindicators of air quality. Generally, in polluted areas (especially where SO 2 is high), lichens do not grow well. Their diversity/abundance is higher in clean air, where- as in highly polluted areas they may even be abs...
Mitochondria act as the powerhouses, it means that the maximum energy (ऊर्जा) in form of ATP is produced within the mitochondria, hence it is also known as Powerhouses of the cell (कोशिका).
During cellular respiration (श्वसन), the initial process takes place in cytoplasm and then in mitochondria.

The most prominent roles of mitochondria are to produce the energy (ऊर्जा) currency of the cell (कोशिका), ATP (adenosine triphosphate), through respiration (श्वसन), and to regulate cellular metabolism. During aerobic respiration, most ATP is formed during oxidative phosphorylation. (f) Golgi body :
Golgi body is also known as Golgi complex or Golgi apparatus. It first observed in 1897 and officially reported in April, 1898 by Camillo Golgi.

The Golgi complex is responsible for processing/ modifying, sorting and packaging certain cellular products such as proteins and lipids that are synthesized by the cell (कोशिका). It consists of stacks of flattened sacs called cisternae. (g) Lysosomes :
Lysosomes are also known as the suicide bags of the cell (कोशिका).

These are membrane-enclosed organelles that contain an array of enzymes capable of breaking down all types of biological polymers-proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids. It functions as the digestive system of the cell (कोशिका) serving both to obsolete material taken up from outside the cell and to digest obsolete components of the cell itself.
Lysosomes also take part in killing the viruses and bacteria (जीवाणु) which have entered within the cell (कोशिका).

A plant cell (कोशिका) is different from animal cell mainly on the basis of the cell wall. The outer shell in a plant cell (which is made from cellulose in green plants) is known as cell wall, which is not found in the animal cell. Except this, green plastids are also found in plant cells while not in animal cells.

Animal cells and plant cells both contain cell (कोशिका) membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus. The nucleus has two major functions. It stores the cell’s hereditary material or DNA and it co-ordinates the cell’s activities within cells. The mitochondrion (plural mitochondria) is a membrane-bound organelle found in most eukaryotic cells. Mitochondria range from 0....

The cell (कोशिका) membrane (also known as plasma (प्लाज्मा) membrane) is a biological membrane that separates the interior of cell from the outside environment. It is composed of two layers of phospholipids and embedded with proteins.

points.html: Heredity (आनुवंशिकता) is the transmission of traits and characteristics via genes/DNA from parents to their offspring.
The offspring get their features, characteristics and genetic information from their mother and father.
Heredity (आनुवंशिकता) explains why offspring resemble parents, while environment also influences traits.
Genetics is a branch of biology that studies the genes, genetic variations and inheritance in living organisms.

During the sexual reproduction process, genetic variations occur due to crossing over, independent assortment/ random segregation, and mutations due to errors in DNA replication. Variations are important because they contribute to evolution (जैव विकास) and provide raw material for natural selection.
Variations are caused due to gene (जीन) mutations, the interaction of genes with the environment and various combinations of genetic material.
Variation can occur through asexual reproduction process too, but these variations are not very noticeable. Gregor Johann Mendel (The Father of Genetics) :
Acquiring characteristics or traits from one generation to the other is nothing but inheritance.

The cell (कोशिका) membrane (also known as plasma (प्लाज्मा) membrane) is a biological membrane that separates the interior of cell from the outside environment. It is composed of two layers of phospholipids and embedded with proteins.

Hybridization was experimented on garden pea plant first by Gregor Mendel. After studying the seven types of qualities of pea, he rendered three laws as– Law of Dominance, Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment.

Gene (जीन) mapping is the method used for determining the location of gene and relative distances between genes on a chromosome (गुणसूत्र). The essence of all genome mapping is to place a collection of molecular markers onto their respective positions on the genome. Molecular markers come in all forms. Genes can be viewed as one special type of genetic markers in t...

A gene (जीन) is the basic physical and functional unit (मात्रक) of heredity (आनुवंशिकता). Genes, which consists of DNA, are the genetic material and unit of heredity. In humans, genes vary in size from a few hundred DNA bases to more than 2 million bases.
Law of Independent Assortment Genome :

A genome is an organism’s complete set of DNA, including all of its genes. Each genome contains all of the information needed to build and maintain that organism. In humans, one copy/haploid set is approx. 3 billion base (क्षार) pairs; most human somatic cells are diploid with two copies in the nucleus, and the human genome also includes mitochondrial DNA; almost every cell (कोशिका) contains a complete copy.

Gene (जीन) Mapping : Gene Mapping describes the methods used to identify the locus of a gene and the distance between genes. The essence of all genome mapping is to place a collection of molecular markers onto their respective positions on the genome. Transposable Elements (TEs) :

Transposable elements or transposon, also known as jumping genes, are DNA sequences that move from one location on the genome to others. Sometimes TEs create or reverse mutations and alter the cell (कोशिका)'s genetic identity and genome size. These elements were first identified by geneticist Barbara McClintock and for this discovery, she was awarded Nobel Prize of Medicine in 1983.
The production of spotted seeds in maize is due to the jumping genes.

Almost half of our DNA sequences are made of jumping genes. Most are inactive; only a small fraction can still mobilize, including in germline/early development contexts. They are important to evolution (जैव विकास). But their mobilization can also cause new mutations that lead to diseases such as haemophilia and cancer. Nucleic Acid (अम्ल) :

The term nucleic acid (अम्ल) is the overall name for DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid). They are composed of nucleotides which are the monomers made of three components : a 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base (क्षार).
Nitrogenous bases are of two types– (i) Purine (ii) Pyrimidine.

A gene (जीन) is the basic physical and functional unit (मात्रक) of heredity (आनुवंशिकता). Change in the base (क्षार) sequence within a gene is called mutation (उत्परिवर्तन). Mutation is the changing of the structure of a gene, resulting in a variant form that may be transmitted to the subsequent generations. Mutation is the ultimate source of all genetic variation, providing the raw material on wh...

The cell (कोशिका) nucleus is a membrane-bound organelle found in eukaryotic cells, acting as the control center and repository of genetic information. The cell nucleus, containing the cell's genetic material (DNA), plays a crucial role in cell reproduction by housing and replicating the DNA, which is then distributed to daughter cells during processes like ...

James Dewey Watson (born April 6, 1928) was an American molecular biologist, geneticist and zoologist, best known as one of the co-discoverers of the structure (double helix model) of DNA in 1953 with Francis Crick. Watson, Crick, and Maurice Wilkins were awarded the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discoveries concerning the "m...
It carries hereditary information from parents to offspring. Human Chromosomes :

Human is unisexual animal. In human, each cell (कोशिका) normally contains 23 pairs of chromosomes, for a total of 46. Twenty-two of these pairs called autosomes in males and females alike. The 23rd pair, the sex chromosomes, differ between males and females.
In males, the chromosomes are 44 + XY (i.e., 46, XY) and in females, chromosomes are 44 + XX (i.e., 46, XX).

At conception, the mother contributes an X chromosome (गुणसूत्र) and the father contributes either X or Y . XX usually results in a female and XY usually results in a male (exceptions can occur in some differences of sex development/ aneuploidy). Some terms about heredity (आनुवंशिकता)

Gene (जीन) : It is the basic unit (मात्रक) of inheritance. It consists of a sequence of DNA in most organisms; RNA is genetic material in some viruses. The genes can mutate and can take two or more alternative forms.

Chromosomes : These are thread-like structures of nucleic acids and protein that are found in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells (prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus). They carry the heredity (आनुवंशिकता) or genetic information in the form of genes. These are made up of nucleoprotein. German anatomist Waldeyer is known for naming the chromosome (गुणसूत्र). The number of chromosomes varies from species to species but it remains constant for a particular species. In most animals, however, any change from the typical chromosome number for a species may be due to genetic disorders.
Genotype : It is the complete heritable genetic identity of an organism. It is the actual set up of alleles that are carried by the organisms.
Phenotype : It is the description of the observable characteristics including internal/functional traits of an organism, the way the genotype is expressed.
Friedrich Miescher first identified and isolated (discovered) DNA in 1869. Double helix model of DNA was given by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953.

Tyrosine or 4-hydroxyphenylalanine is one of the 22 amino acids that are used by cells to synthesize proteins. Its codons are UAC and UAU. It is a non-essential amino acid (अम्ल) with a polar side group. It was first discovered in 1846 by German chemist Justus von Liebig in the protein casein from cheese. It is called tyrosyl when referred to as a functio...
The deoxyribose is sugar found in DNA. It is a variant of five carbon sugar called ribose. The DNA is an informational molecule (अणु) found mainly in the nucleus of the cell (कोशिका).
Karyotypes of many species of the genus Sceloporus support the generalization that there are no morphologically recognizable sex chromosomes in lizards.

In humans, each cell (कोशिका) normally contains 23 pairs of chromosomes, a total of 46. Twenty-two of these pairs called autosomes which are the same in both males and females. The 23rd pair, the sex chromosomes differ between males and females. Females have two copies of the X chromosome (गुणसूत्र) (XX) while males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY).

points.html: Over the years, chemical fertilisers have helped farmers increase crop production to meet rising demand. However, excessive and continuous use of chemical fertilisers can cause water pollution and may reduce soil fertility by harming soil microorganisms and by not replenishing organic matter in the soil. Hence, there is a growing push towards organic and other sustainable farming approaches, including the use of biofertilizers.

Biofertilizers are beneficial microorganisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil and improve nutrient availability to plants. They are used to replenish soil nutrients and reduce dependence on chemical fertilisers, thereby helping in more environment-friendly crop production. Types of Biofertilizers :
Following are the types of biofertilizers–

Biofertilizers are products that contain living or dormant beneficial microorganisms (such as Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum, phosphate-solubilizing Bacillus, etc.) which, when applied to seeds/soil, enhance nutrient availability. Organic manures or green manures are nutrient sources but are not biofertilizers.

Biofertilizers are defined as preparations containing living cells or latent cells of efficient strains of microorganisms that help crop plants uptake of nutrients, by their interactions in the rhizosphere when applied through seed or soil. They accelerate certain microbial processes in the soil which aug- ment the extent of availability of nutrien...
Nostoc, Anabaena and Azotobacter are nitrogen-fixing organisms while mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association between a fungus (कवक) and a plant.

There are two types of bone marrow : (i) Yellow bone marrow which contains adipose tissue and triglycerides stored in the adipocytes of this tissue can be released to serve as a source of energy (ऊर्जा) for other tissues of the body and (ii) Red bone marrow, where the production of blood cells (named hematopoiesis, hemato = "blood", poiesis = "to make") takes place. Digestion is a form of catabolism that is often divided into two processes based on how food is broken down : mechanical and chemical digestion.

The number of bones in an adult human body is 206. The body of a child has about 300 bones at birth, which decreases to 206 bones by adulthood after some bones have fused together. Together these bones form the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton.

The stapes is the lightest stirrup-shaped bone and the smallest bone in the human body found in the middle of humans ears. While femur is the largest bone in the human body. It is located in the upper leg which connects the knee at one end and fits into the hip socket at the other.

The joint where the neck joins the head is a pivot (pivotal) joint, also known as a rotary joint, allowing for head rotation and some flexion and extension. A pivot joint is a type of synovial joint where a cylindrical bone rotates within a ring-shaped bone, allowing for rotational movement along a single axis.
